title: Chaitanya takes the names to the street
hookLine: a grammar teacher whose every lesson turns into Krishna
carry: kirtan: god's names, a song anyone can join
tomorrow: Humbler than a blade of grass

cards: A grammar teacher in Bengal has a problem. His students come to learn Sanskrit grammar, and every rule he explains turns into Krishna. A verb ending?
Krishna. A noun? One of Krishna's names.

Tradition says this young teacher, Nimai, was known in his town of Navadvipa as a brilliant scholar and a fierce debater. Then he went on pilgrimage to Gaya, and came home unable to talk about anything else.
His students, the story goes, closed their books and left. He let them go. He had found something louder than grammar.

teach.b: Nimai is the man remembered as Chaitanya.

teach.h: THE DOORS OPEN TO THE LANES.
teach.b: Back home, he and his friends began to gather at night in the courtyard of a devotee named Shrivasa, doors shut, singing God's names together. Drums, cymbals, one voice leading, everyone answering.
That's kirtan: praise sung out loud, together, the names repeated again and again. Then the doors opened.
Chaitanya's companions took the singing into the lanes of Navadvipa, a procession moving from house to house, and whoever heard it could fall in behind.
At its center his tradition places one chant: Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.
Nothing but names, calling and calling.

His tradition teaches that in this age, the Kali Yuga, singing the names of God is the surest path of all. What's radical is how little it asks. No Sanskrit grammar, no years of study, no temple door to get through.

You need a voice, or even just ears and the willingness to answer. His followers in Bengal, the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, remember him dancing as he sang, weeping, falling to the ground, his whole body caught up in the names.
They also hold that he was more than a saint: Krishna himself, joined with Radha, come to taste his own love from the inside. Others honor him as a great teacher of devotion.
Either way, what he gave the street was the same: a song anyone could join on the first try.

how: In Gaudiya Vaishnava temples and homes, kirtan is sung with drums and hand cymbals, one voice leading and the group answering, and street processions of chanting, called nagar kirtan, still pass through towns and cities.

s: Chaitanya's kirtan stayed behind closed doors
it began in a courtyard at night, then went out into the lanes of Navadvipa.
joining kirtan takes years of study
one voice leads and everyone answers; it asks for a voice, or just ears.
tradition says his students left because every lesson turned into Krishna
after Gaya, every rule of grammar became Krishna, and the students closed their books.

games.q: you're a celebrated young scholar, home from pilgrimage, and all you can talk about is Krishna. your students want grammar. what do you do?
o: go back to teaching grammar as before.
let the students go, and start singing the names.
write a learned book proving Krishna is in grammar.
games.why: tradition says the students left and Nimai let them go. the nights of singing in Shrivasa's courtyard came next, and then the street.

practice: Kirtan is a call and an answer, so try it. Say a name of God softly, the leader's line: Hari, or Krishna, or Rama, or a name your family uses. Then answer it yourself, a little more softly, the way the crowd would.
Keep the call and the answer going, gently, for a few rounds; that's how kirtan begins. If you don't pray, call and answer with one soft sound, and notice how easy it is to join.

wordCard.voice: Kirtan. Praise sung aloud, God's names repeated together with drums and cymbals, which Chaitanya took out of a closed courtyard and into the street.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi, in Devanagari: praise sung aloud, God's names sung together.

carryVoice: Your line: kirtan, God's names, a song anyone can join. All it asks is a voice, or even just ears. Until tomorrow.
